summary: Suspicious IAM approval chain activations after user reported phishing attachment
description: Issue summary: On 2026-03-12 morning a Redwood employee reported a suspicious email with a Microsoft Office attachment. Shortly after, automated alerts flagged multiple 'approval' events in IAM for low-privilege service principals and new email forwarding rules created for several user accounts. Impact: Potential privilege escalation or lateral movement; unknown scope. Initial detection: End user in #security-reports Slack uploaded the attachment and reported unusual pop-ups. Automated ABAC/Approval-monitoring generated alerts at 2026-03-12T08:44Z. Observed artifacts: suspicious attachment headers (X-MS-Exchange-Organization-AuthAs: Anonymous), email message IDs, a small burst of IAM approval webhooks (3 approvals in 4 minutes), and three mailbox forwarding rules created in quick succession. Scope estimate: 7 user mailboxes touched, 2 service principals triggered approval flows, no obvious data exfil observed in S3/Blob access logs so far. Steps taken so far: (1) Disabled affected mailbox forwarding rules; (2) Revoked active tokens for the two affected service principals; (3) Blocked the sending IP at email gateway; (4) Opened this internal incident ticket and paged Security on-call. Next steps: complete hunt for lateral movement, rotate credentials for any service principal with unexpected approvals, and initiate user phishing awareness and password resets as needed.
investigation: Timeline and findings: 2026-03-12 08:41Z - user reported attachment; 08:44Z - approval-monitoring alert for sp-prod-etl (approval path: user -> approver-bot -> sp-prod-etl); 08:46Z - mailbox-forwarding creation event for user alice@redwood.com and bob@redwood.com; 08:52Z - SRE observed two short-lived console sessions from an internal IP range that is not usually active for these users. Hypotheses: (A) attachment contained link that initiated OAuth approval via malicious consent screen (consent phishing); (B) session cookie capture led to approval API calls from attacker infrastructure; (C) forged approval webhooks from compromised CI runner. Evidence collected: email headers, raw attachment saved to /sec/artifacts/INT-17350/, IAM approval audit logs (IDs: apr-20260312-01..03), IP addresses 35.201.112.43 and 3.120.210.9 correlating to cloud provider regions not normally used by our teams. Tools and queries used: "search-logs --start 2026-03-12T07:00Z --end 2026-03-12T10:00Z 'approval'"; Splunk dashboard link: https://splunk.redwood.com/en-US/app/search?sid=165. Runbook consulted: Phishing-Triage-Runbook (confluence link above). Partial findings: approvals appear to have been programmatically triggered (no interactive console fingerprints), but tokens were short-lived. No direct PRs or code changes correlated to the time window; CI runners were checked and no anomalies found.
comments: 2026-03-12 09:05 - Jonah Patel: Acknowledged; I'm isolating the two service principals and rotating secrets. Placing temporary deny rules on approval webhook endpoint.
2026-03-12 09:22 - Security On-call (Maya Chen): Blocking sender and requesting full mailstore export for affected mailboxes. Notifying Legal to prepare potential breach notification requirements.
2026-03-12 10:10 - Alice (reporting user): I opened the attachment by mistake, it asked me to 'Allow Redwood App' and I clicked Allow. I do not recall entering credentials.
2026-03-12 13:45 - Jonah Patel: Revoked tokens for sp-prod-etl and sp-analytics. No new approval events after 12:15Z. Continuing hunt for suspicious sessions.
resolution: Containment actions applied: removed forwarding rules on 7 mailboxes, revoked affected service principal tokens, temporarily disabled approval webhook endpoint, blocked two outbound IPs at the perimeter. Short-term mitigation: force password reset for 7 users and require 2FA revalidation; rotate credentials for all service principals used in the ETL/analytics group. Owner: Security Team. Long-term follow-ups: (1) Harden approval webhook with HMAC verification and stricter scopes; (2) add automated detection for rapid approval bursts; (3) update phishing training to cover OAuth consent scams. Incident remains open pending full audit and confirmation of no additional compromised accounts.
